title: Master Class | Smith–Morra Gambit | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Black plays a Queen's Gambit Declined — the original solid choice.
White fianchettoes with g3 instead — not dangerous, but because it does not challenge the centre at once...
...Black gets to bring the bishop out to f5 first, outside the pawn chain, Caro-Kann style — and only then play e6.
The bishop sits outside the chain now — an ideal, London-type setup.
In a London setup Black often plays h6, giving the bishop luft on h7 and taking the sting out of a knight to h4.
The knight to c3 is a classic inaccuracy at this level — it blocks the c-pawn from reaching c4.
Black's centre is as solid as it gets, with the c5 lever even available. Just complete development.
White is not threatening e4 — Black has defended it three times, and White attacks it only twice.
Now Black is ready for c5. And the knight to h4...
...is exactly why h6 was played — the bishop simply steps to h7.

White strikes with e4, opening the centre — a legitimate idea, but it will not serve him well. The simplest reply is to take everything on e4; note how his king weakens without the fianchetto bishop, and the idea of taking on h4 is in the air.
Using the fact that this knight can be captured to ruin White's structure, Black takes on e4.
There is an intermediate move — taking on h4 first — and Black is up a pawn. White's clever try was the knight to c5, but he just takes.

Black recaptures, wrecking White's pawn structure. Careful, though — Black cannot grab back here, because White takes on b7 and wins the exchange; Black plays meat-and-potatoes chess, not speculative sacs.
The zen recapture — the knight to c6, developing while doing the same job. For the small price of doubled pawns, Black gets opposite-coloured bishops, which favour the attacker in the middlegame.
White takes the bishop with check — but Black is happily forking two pawns in return.
The rook to e4 is strong, and now it is time to make things go boom. White's bishop is still undeveloped, so his king is under-defended — pry the centre open and White pays.
e5 is possible, but f5 is more forcing — it drives the rook, and after it moves, e5 wins. If White takes on e6, the knight takes on d4 with discovered-check ideas — very nasty.

White cannot grab the pawn because his queen is undefended — which is exactly why Black must act with urgency: the moment the bishop develops, the queen is covered and the discovered-attack tactics vanish.
Nothing fancy needed — bring the last rook into play, setting up an x-ray against the queen.

Careful with the checks — the queen can take them. The real threat is the knight to b3, hitting the rook in the corner. And keep an eye on g7: if White's queen could ever reach a square hitting g7 it would be mate — but look carefully, it cannot.

Black grabs the rook and it is over — the king is a touch airy, but Black is simply winning. There is even a forced mate: a queen check, and after the rook drops back, the queen to e4 is mate — the hanging pieces do not matter.

The one real moment was the knight takes on e4 and then the bishop takes on h4. White's correct try was the knight to c5, counter-attacking b7 — a double-edged position — but Black relied on him to miss it. This setup with the knight sitting on c3 is risky for White: without e4 he has no plan, while Black keeps the c5 lever in reserve.
